Resistance, Enactment, and Interpretation: A Self-Analytic Study

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

17 Hammond Street
Cambridge, MA 02138-1915

Henry Smith  

Whenever we write about psychoanalytic work we introduce an artifact. The work described can never convey the complexity of the work itself, even in the hands of so gifted a writer as Ted Jacobs.

In describing anything we make a selection. That selection in our writing may resemble the selections we make for observation and comment in the office, but the relationship between the two is never exact. Furthermore, in isolating any part of the work for observation and description we freeze it, reify it, and give it a definition that may suggest the work is made up of a linear series of discrete entities, such as defenses, drive derivatives, or, for that matter, enactments, rather than forces and processes in motion. These entities are, in part, necessary artifacts of observation and description.

The entities we describe allow others to observe them in their work—or disagree with them and describe something different—but they also make our literature appear cleaner, tidier, and more surefooted than our observations in the office can ever be. And they identify certain writers with certain phenomena or types of interventions, Arlow (1991) with the interpretation of unconscious fantasy, for example; Schwaber (1986) with the observation of a patient's shifts in state; and Jacobs (1991) with the interplay of enactments.

Howard Levine Issue Editor

Howard Levine

Howard Levine  

In November of 1994, the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (BPSI) presented a 2-day symposium entitled “New Psychoanalytic Perspectives on the Treatment of Sexual Trauma.”1 The goal of this meeting was to create a forum in which some of the foremost contributors to the psychoanalytic literature in the area of sexual trauma could draw upon their work with infants, children, adolescents, and adults to explore

how childhood trauma becomes represented in the mind;

the unique pathogenicity of childhood sexual trauma;

problems of validation of patient memories and therapist reconstructions, including the possibility of false memories and their implications for treatment;

the analytic treatment of childhood sexual trauma and incest in children and adults; and

risk factors, subjective experience, pathological consequences, prevention and repair of patient-therapist sexual boundary violations.

The articles that follow represent the majority of the papers presented at the Boston Symposium. (Unfortunately, two additional presentations, those of Daniel Schacter, “Implicit Memory, Explicit Memory and False Memory: A Cognitive Neuroscience Perspective,” and Jody M. Davies, “On Memory and False Memory: Dissociation, Repression and Reality Testing in the Countertransference,” could not be included in the present volume.)

Epilogue

Dorthy Levinson M.S.W. Issue Editor and Janet Droga M.S.W. Issue Editor

Janet Droga

Janet Droga  

It is our view that the experienced linking of mind and body may only be understood in the context of human relatedness in which it is embedded. Chronic failures of attunement during development interfere with the ability to link and integrate somatic, sensory, motoric, and cognitive aspects of experience with symbolic, affectively toned self and object images. The result is an inner world characterized by severe dissociations reflecting the fragmenting effect of interactions with invalidating and abusive caregivers.

While we agree that somatization may be a symptom of defensive or structural regression, our clinical observations suggest an additional possibility, namely, that somatization may also represent the first perceivable registering of actual subjective experience. In this context, we see dissociated bodily states as attempts at schematization of traumatically invalidated subjective worlds. In this instance, somatization occurs in a context of validating acceptance and responsiveness. It constitutes a developmental achievement in the process of self-integration.

When a patient appears in our consulting room with somatic symptoms or develops them during the analysis, we may very well be seeing a desperate attempt to communicate a “personal holocaust.” Hopefully, we now can use a new lexicon for an expanded repertoire of registering their meanings. All too often, instances of somatization that do not yield to a particular theoretical formulation are considered unanalyzable and relegated to the internist. We underscore the need for studying alternative possibilities for those bodily states not yet understood in theory. These should not be considered unanalyzable and/or dismissed as a negative therapeutic reaction, thus blaming the patient for the limitations of our knowledge. We hope that this volume of Psychoanalytic Inquiry brings us further toward accomplishing that goal.

The essays in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry raise questions that are vital for us as concerned citizens, as researchers, as teachers, as clinicians. They are questions about the varying effects of sexual trauma on individuals and about our responses to them. The questions raised are also about the nature of memory and about our own ways of understanding and treating those who have experienced sexual trauma. These questions do not lend themselves to easy answers or simple explanations. In fact, the matter is so complex that it is often hard to know exactly where to begin

For me, one starting place in trying to organize my thinking about sexual trauma and its treatment is a dream of Freud's. In the now famous “Irma dream”—something happens that is relevant to the subject at hand. You will remember that Freud felt criticized by a colleague who reported to Freud that one of Freud's patients, Emma Eckstein (Irma in Freud's dream) was still unwell despite psychoanalytic treatment. That night, Freud had a strange and complicated dream that he interpreted as being an argument for Irma's continuing difficulties not being his fault. In chapter 2 of The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) he masterfully elaborates the wish-fulfilling and narcissistic bases of his Irma dream—and of all our dreams. Schur (1972) was later to point out that it was also a dream in which Freud struggles with recognizing and disguising the significance of his colleague Fliess's medical mistreatment. Fliess

Susan Lazar Issue Editor

Susan Lazar

Susan Lazar  

Making the case for extended dynamic psychotherapy is difficult, important, and possible. In these times of the “quick fix” and profit-driven managed care, the difficulty arises from the received wisdom that psychoanalysis and long-term dynamic treatment are “out” and medications and brief treatments are “in.” In many quarters, psychoanalytic thinking has fallen into disrepute while psychoanalytic treatments have suffered from a relative paucity of outcome research. Are psychoanalytic theory and practice destined for an early demise after one brief century of ascent and decline?

As the articles in this special supplemental issue attest, however, psychodynamic treatments have a unique value for certain patients, which is supported by a growing body of evidence. In particular:

There are significant groups of patients who will not improve without extended psychotherapy.

When information similar to that in this issue about the efficacy and cost effectiveness of psychotherapy was presented to policymakers during the health care reform initiative in 1993, virtual parity for outpatient psychotherapy benefits with all other medical care was provided both in the Democratic and Republican health care reform proposals. Similar data have led to the protection of psychotherapy benefits in laws in Virginia, Maryland, and the District of Columbia.

Most of the American public now support the idea of providing necessary mental health care.

Most Americans with psychiatric disorders, including those requiring extended dynamic psychotherapy, do not receive the care they need. This neglect leads to needless suffering and the loss of literally billions of dollars in lost wages, unnecessary medical and surgical services for psychosomatic complaints, and increased psychiatric hospital care.

Four prototypical patient profiles will serve to illustrate some common and problematic situations with mental illness that many Americans face.

A is an 11-year-old boy with an anxiety disorder. Despite his above-average intelligence, he has difficulty reading and has already repeated the fourth grade. Antianxiety medications have been of some help, at times, in controlling his anxiety symptoms, but they are sedating, potentially addicting, and cannot address the underlying problem.

Mrs. B is a 32-year-old pregnant, working mother of two, who has a major depression. Although she has a family history of depression, her recurrent illness began with the death of her father when she was 10. Intermittently depressed as a child, she has nevertheless become well-educated and has married, and had two children. Although her income is very important in sustaining her family, like many patients with major depression, she cannot work.

Patricia Harney  

Victimization by interpersonal violence has become a normative event for U.S. citizens. Nationwide investigations conducted during the last twenty years have documented the widespread prevalence of child physical abuse, child sexual abuse, incest, adolescent and adult-incident rape, domestic violence, and other crimes of violence (e.g., Russell, 1984; Wyatt, 1985; Koss, Gidycz, and Wiesniewski, 1987; National Center on Child Abuse and Neglect, 1988; Boney-McCoy and Finkelhor, 1995). An equally ample literature has developed to document the potentially devastating consequences of these events. Research has established, for example, that victims can suffer lasting impairments in their physical, psychological, and interpersonal functioning (Browne and Finkelhor, 1986; Stein et al., 1988; Herman, 1992; Briere and Runtz, 1993). Those whose lives have been shattered by physical and sexual violence include an alarming number of women and children who have not found safe harbor even in their own homes (National Victims Center, 1992; Koss, 1993). Moreover, violence in the home and on the streets has become a social and public health problem that not only has direct, personal consequences for victims, but also entails substantial costs to the larger society.

Harold Eist MD

Harold Eist

5705 Rossmore Drive
Bethesda, MD 20814

Harold Eist  

In America prior to the 1930s, it was considered prudent to put aside a portion of the family income to cover the cost of medical care. Those families decimated by major illnesses were viewed moralistically as improvident and the proper object of fiscal counseling.

During the depression in the early 1930s, it become increasingly evident that only the wealthy could ensure the availability of a sufficiency of funds to cover the costs of severe or catastrophic illnesses.

The American Hospital Association (AHA) as early as 1927, had as its goal “the provision of hospitalization for the patient of moderate means, consisting of 80% of the entire population.” Hospitalization plans, it was indicated by the AHA, which was the primary funder of what was to become Blue Cross/Blue Shield, should be available “for all persons regardless of their ability to pay” and were designed to reach those employed at “low incomes who would otherwise require the aid of philanthropy or taxation” (Law, 1974). (Currently, the Republican leader of the House of Representatives and his disciples want to remove the floor of suffering, misery, and degradation below which we would previously allow no American to fall and replace what Medicaid has provided with “philanthropy.”)

The hospitals were strong advocates for hospital insurance out of self-interest, as well as out of concern for the public, for they found that they, too, were suffering financially during the depression.

Dr. Eist is President, American Psychiatric Association.

The Human Toll: Managed Care's Restriction of Access to Mental Health Services

Barbara Shapard L.C.S.W.

Barbara Shapard

2727 N. Norwood Street
Arlington, VA 22207

Barbara Shapard  

Since the 1980s, the cost control measures instituted by managed care practices for health care have curtailed access to all medical services. This cost control trend has resulted in an increasing burden, especially for the vulnerable users of mental health services.

The protocols practiced by managed care severely restrict both the frequency and length of mental health treatment. Generally, managed care limits treatment from three to 20 visits, effectively excluding coverage for severe or chronic mental illness, which requires long-term care (Welch, 1994). In contrast, there are numerous studies documenting the needs of certain patient groups for extended psychotherapy. The research suggests need for 1-212 years of psychotherapy for patients with borderline personality disorder and 212 or more years for those with dissociative disorder and the need for the ongoing availability of psychotherapy for patients with depression (Klerman et al., 1974; Kluft, 1988; Putman, 1989; Ross, 1989; Frank et al., 1991; Stevenson and Meares, 1992; Fonagy and Target, 1992; Lowenstein and Putman, 1993; Lanktree and Briere, 1993; Barach, 1994). The vignettes below detail the consequences of limitations by managed care practices of both inpatient and outpatient mental health treatment.

Ms. Shapard is a member of the Faculty, Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Program, Psychoanalytic Foundation of Washington, DC; Clinical Instructor, Psychiatry, Georgetown University; and Faculty, Institute for Contemporary Psychotherapy.

Epilogue

Arnold Rachman Issue Editor

Arnold Rachman

Arnold Rachman  

Our mission in this special issue, honoring Sándor Ferenczi, was to acquaint the present generation of psychotherapists and psychoanalysts with his theory and method because his work had been suppressed and removed from mainstream psychoanalysis (Rachman, 1989, 1993, 1994, 1997). His ideas and methods, particularly of his last clinical period, profoundly disturbed Freud and the analytic community and contributed to a trauma (Balint, 1968) that lasted from his last presentation, “The Confusion of Tongues” (Ferenczi, 1933) until about the early 1980s (Rachman, 1997). During the 50-year period, generations of psychotherapists and psychoanalysts were deprived of his contributions, since they were not taught either in traditional analytic or alternative institutes (Rachman, 1997). Because his ideas were so clinically sound, they found their way into the major dissident frameworks of psychoanalysis, such as object relations, interpersonal psychoanalysis, and self psychology. Because his humanistic method was considered “not psychoanalysis,” his ideas could not be openly acknowledged without facing rejection by the analytic establishment. Nevertheless, these contributions were of such a magnitude that eventually they would be rediscovered when the climate in psychoanalysis was less oppressive and when the limitations of orthodoxy became inescapable. For example, the concept of empathy, which Ferenczi introduced into psychoanalysis in 1928 (Ferenczi, 1928), was lost to mainstream psychoanalysis. Various psychoanalytic dissidents who came after Ferenczi (first Sullivan, then Winnicott, and finally Kohut) found that empathy was central to their clinical work. Now, empathy is well established in liberal psychoanalysis, but Ferenczi's contributions are rarely mentioned (Rachman, 1988).

Ferenczi's role in the history of psychoanalysis brings to the foreground many neglected aspects of psychoanalytic inquiry. Issues of power, control, and status so evident in the suffering of individuals was also relevant in the relationship of the pioneers of psychoanalysis.

The Effectiveness of Dynamic Psychotherapy for Depression

Susan Lazar MD

Susan Lazar

9104 Quintana Drive
Bethesda, MD 20817

Susan Lazar  

Affective illness affects 11 percent of the adult American population every year and nearly 20 percent at some point during their lifetime. The yearly prevalence breaks down into 10.33 percent for major depression, 2.5 percent for dysthymia, and 11.3 percent for all affective illness (Kessler et al., 1994). The yearly cost of depressive illness is $43.7 billion. Of this total, $12.4 billion is in direct costs for the treatment of depression, including inpatient and outpatient psychiatric services, rehabilitation, and medications. The indirect costs, $31.3 billion, are fully three-fourths of the total and include $7.5 billion from earnings lost due to suicide, $11.7 billion due to absenteeism from work, and $12.1 billion from a loss of productive capacity (Greenberg et al., 1993). One study has found that patients with major depression have a 4.78 greater risk of disability and patients with minor depression have a 1.55 greater risk of disability than those without illness (Broadhead et al., 1990). In addition, patients with depression incur nearly double the medical costs of those without (Simon et al., 1995) and are associated with as much or more functional disability than hypertension, diabetes, advanced coronary artery disease, angina, back problems, arthritis, pulmonary disease, and gastrointestinal disease (Wells et al., 1989).

Dr. Lazar is Supervising and Training Analyst, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Georgetown University School of Medicine, and George Washington University School of Medicine.

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

The preceding papers reveal an image of the analytic situation far different from that portrayed in the literature of the past. The analyst we have seen is active, engaged, and contributing significantly to the patient's experiences. The analyst is seen as interactive, using herself or himself to assist in orienting, perceiving, and understanding the analytic material. The analyst is not only observer, interpreter, and provider of a new relationship, he or she is a participant in a mutual experience of working through and growth. This modified view of the analyst applies to the supervisory situation as well as to the analytic one.

In his response to the Essays, Jacobs observes that psychoanalysis has been criticized for being impervious to change, yet the current trend of increased attention to the experience of the analyst in the analytic situation strongly contradicts this view. The contents of this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry further demonstrates Jacobs's observation and points to the vitality and excitement of psychoanalysis today.

Borderline Personality Disorder and Rational Managed Care Policy

Glen Gabbard MD

Glen Gabbard

P.O. Box 829
Topeka, KS 66601-0829

Glen Gabbard  

Under the vast majority of managed care arrangements, the psychotherapy of patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD) is severely limited. In some cases, treatment of such patients is entirely eliminated based on a policy of only reimbursing treatment of Axis-I conditions. Given that approximately 23 percent of inpatients and 11 percent of outpatients suffer from BPD (Widiger and Frances, 1989), this stipulation leaves a great many severely disturbed individuals without adequate treatment.

Other managed care companies may allow anywhere from 6 to 30 psychotherapy sessions for borderline patients. While there are no hard data to support the efficacy of such brief treatments with borderline patients, the limits are generally rationalized based on the notion that patients with BPD are “bottomless pits” who will be in treatment indefinitely if given the opportunity for more extended treatment. This practice of setting arbitrary session limits is a recipe for disaster with many patients. By the very nature of their psychopathology, borderline patients live with an undercurrent of dread that, at any moment, they will be abandoned.

Dr. Gabbard is Bessie Walker Callaway Distinguished Professor of Psychoanalysis and Education, Karl Menninger School of Psychiatry and Mental Health Sciences; Training and Supervising Analyst, Topeka Institute for Psychoanalysis; and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of Kansas School of Medicine, Wichita.

Prepared for a symposium entitled “Personality Disorders in the Managed Care Era” presented at the annual meeting of the American Psychiatric Association, May 25, 1994.

Epilogue: Sexual Trauma: Where Do We Stand?

Howard Levine Issue Editor

Howard Levine

Howard Levine  

In recent years, our society has undergone a profound reorientation in our awareness of childhood sexual abuse and incest. Although analysts had always recognized the existence of these problems, prior to the past decade, they had not paid sufficient specific attention to them (Levine, 1990). For example, it was only a few years ago that I had occasion to note that the psychoanalytic literature in this area had “barely begun to emerge. In particular, questions of technique and studies of the analytic process in adults who were sexually abused as children [had] yet to be thoroughly raised and examined” (Levine, 1990, p. 4).

Given the deluge of books and articles on this subject that have subsequently appeared, such a statement no longer applies. Through careful observation and reporting of clinical experience, numerous authors, of which our contributors are among the foremost, have significantly advanced our knowledge of the consequences and treatment of childhood sexual abuse. Clearly, the papers presented in this volume will further add to our understanding and to the expansion of our therapeutic efforts.

In spite of all that we have learned, however, we are left with much that remains to be understood. In this issue, for example, despite the significant contributions made by Parens' description of the organizing power of oedipal conflicts on the structure of posttraumatic pathology, Novick's moving presentation and insightful discussion of the ego disruption caused by sexual trauma in her little patient, Taylor, and Coates and Moore's discussion of the effects of nonsexual trauma on gender identity formation, we remain painfully aware that we have only begun to address questions of major developmental import.

Epilogue

Susan Lazar Issue Editor

Susan Lazar

Susan Lazar  

Our contributors have provided us with a wealth of vital information about the extent of mental illness in our country, the vast waste from the neglect of psychiatric patients and the savings that could be realized by the ready availability of medically necessary psychotherapy without arbitrary restrictions. We have seen data about the cost effectiveness of extended psychotherapy for patients with borderline personality disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, the medically ill, depressed patients, and child patients. Actuarial studies in this country and in Germany attest to the cost savings realized when patients have access to appropriate length and intensity of dynamic psychotherapy. Indeed, in some diagnostic groups, extended intensive psychotherapy is vital to recovery.

The obstacles to the support of dynamic psychotherapy include a fast-paced, “sound bite” culture that is blind to the slow and subtle processes of long-term psychotherapy. The difficulty in funding and pursuing controlled clinical trials for long-term treatments has led to a relative paucity of convincing research results. Perhaps the most formidable obstacle has been profit-driven insurance practices that have ravaged appropriate medical services of every type and have found psychiatric patients an especially vulnerable population from whom it is easy to withhold care in the interest of short-term profits. These patients are neglected, however, at the peril of society at large, which picks up the tab in increased disability payments, decreased productivity, and increased medical and surgical costs, to say nothing of increased suicides and immeasurable, unnecessary human suffering.

On the other hand, experience of the last few years demonstrates that legislative bodies and the public at large are open and responsive to the good data that are available. It is up to advocates of psychotherapy to bring our best arguments to the attention of policymakers and to the American people.

Prologue

Arnold Rachman Issue Editor

Arnold Rachman

Arnold Rachman  

This edition of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is a landmark publication in that it contributes to the “Ferenczi Renaissance” (the contemporary reconsideration of Ferenczi as a significant figure in psychoanalysis) by devoting an entire professional journal to a focus on his ideas, methods, and relationships. Rediscovery of Sándor Ferenczi and his legacy to psychoanalysis has been necessary because his work was deliberately suppressed and his character maligned in a campaign to discredit him as a significant figure and remove him from mainstream psychoanalysis. Ferenczi's fate constitutes one of the darkest and most tragic periods in psychoanalytic history. It is a privilege to contribute to a continued reevaluation of his ideas and methods that can only enrich contemporary psychoanalysis, as well as allow Ferenczi to gain the recognition he deserves as one of the most talented clinicians in the history of our field. While Freud was the theoretical genius of psychoanalysis, as well as its founder, one could say Ferenczi was the clinical genius and the inspiration for modern analytic technique.

We have been very fortunate to gather together an international group of Ferenczi scholars, from Austria, France, Hungary, Switzerland and the United States, who represent orientations that Ferenczi influenced: Freudian, interpersonal, object relations, relational, and self psychology.

Claude Lorin brings us a fascinating excursion into the discovery of Ferenczi's earliest writings in the Hungarian medical journal Gyogyazat, before Ferenczi joined Freud as a collaborator. Lorin believes this early material shows the pre-Freudian Ferenczi who was a creative pioneer in psychiatry and psychotherapy before he began collaborating with Freud.

John Gedo reexamines one of Ferenczi's classic monographs, The Development of Psychoanalysis, coauthored with Otto Rank in 1924.

Ego Disruption in an Abused Little Girl

Kerry Novick MA

Kerry Novick

617 Stratford
Ann Arbor, MI 48104

Kerry Novick  

This is the story of the treatment of a little girl I shall call Taylor. When I met her she was just 5. She did not know how to pretend, but played mechanically, in a way that was deeply boring. Nothing in her games happened in an order that made sense to me, and Taylor did not seem to notice that sometimes the dolls ate breakfast before they went to sleep or arrived at school before they got into the car. She liked to line up and sort the toys but could not communicated the basis for the categories. Taylor did only what she wanted, but she also wanted to know and perform what would placate the grownups. The puzzle was to understand the meaning and aetiology of this appearance of profound dissociation and to help Taylor achieve integration of her developing ego, so that it might effectively mediate between her impulses and the outside world.

But the outside world had already impinged inappropriately on Taylor. Working with children can be very unlike our frequent predicament with adult patients, who remember or suspect abuse in their past or whose treatment uncovers such a possibility. With Taylor, the facts were clear that her history contained numerous evidences of abuse of different kinds. So at the start we had definite information on the one hand and, on the other, a child who was not functioning adequately. One of the tasks of evaluation and treatment was to understand the connections between Taylor's history and her current functioning.

Ms. Novick is a member of the Faculty, Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute, and Clinical Director, Allen Creek Preschool.

The Need for Psychotherapy in the Medically Ill

David Spiegel MD and Susan Lazar MD

Susan Lazar

Stanford, CA 94305

9104 Quintana Drive
Bethesda, MD 20817

Susan Lazar  

Many medical and surgical patients have a need for psychotherapy, both because of a high prevalence of psychiatric disorders in this population and secondarily because of the inherent stress of serious illness. Six percent of patients in primary care settings and 11 percent of medical inpatients have a diagnosis of major depression (Katon and Sullivan, 1990). In addition, nearly half of all cancer patients have a diagnosable psychiatric disorder (Derogatis, Morrow, and Fetting, 1983).

Psychotherapy provides a source both of support and interpersonal connection. The need for this among the medically ill is illustrated by the fact that the relationship between social isolation and risk of death is as great as smoking or elevated serum cholesterol and mortality (House, Landis, and Umberson, 1988). In addition, social stress such as job loss or the death of a loved one is associated in several studies with a higher incidence of malignancy and higher relapse rates in cancer patients.

Patients with multiple physical symptoms but no diagnosable physical disease have nine times the average per capita medical care cost (Smith, Monson, and Ray, 1986)

Dr. Spiegel is Professor of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University School of Medicine.

Owen Renik  

The Use of the Self is enormously instructive and a delight to read. Although much of the book is taken from previously published papers, it does not come across as a rehash of already familiar material. Rather, the aggregate gives the reader an opportunity to review and consider the nature of Ted Jacobs's contribution to our contemporary understanding of how an analyst participates in analytic work.

One of the things I noticed immediately is that Ted communicates mainly by example: by far the greatest part of what he has written consists of a series of clinical narratives—the kind of rich, graceful, evocative accounts of an analyst's clinical experience for which Ted is deservedly renowned. Theoretical discussion is, by contrast, relatively sparse, which is interesting because through his vignettes Ted gives us a view of the analyst, with all his or her personal psychology in operation, contributing to a successful psychoanalytic process that is, in my view, even more advanced than the conception of technique that seems to inform the accompanying commentary. As a theoretician Ted is certainly a liberal, but as a clinical illustrator I am convinced that he breaks new ground. In a way, this reflects the state of psychoanalytic affairs in general: it is considerably easier for us to be effective in comparing notes anecdotally about particular clinical events—in supervision, for example—than when we try to formulate a really useful, systematic, and explicit theory of analytic technique.

Dr. Renik is Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Dorthy Levinson M.S.W. Issue Editor and Janet Droga M.S.W. Issue Editor

Janet Droga

Janet Droga  

The inspiration for assembling a group of papers on the relationship between bodily experience and mental states came from reflections on clinical work. One of us (D.M.L.) came upon an unexpected development in the course of psychoanalytic treatment and found that the appearance or exacerbation of somatic symptoms proved to be a signal that dissociated and formerly invalidated traumatic memories and the affects associated with them, were crystallizing and being retrieved in the analysis. These clinical observations were in sharp contrast to the vast majority of psychoanalytic concepts regarding somatization. The appearance of somatic symptoms is generally explained as a sign of regression resulting either from the patient's defensive maneuvers or from the patient's reaction to a failure in empathy on the part of caregivers during development or on the part of the analyst in the course of treatment. In this instance, the emergence of somatic symptoms constituted a developmental achievement in the context of a validating, archaic bond with the analyst. Subsequently, these symptoms disappeared when the analyst was able to fathom, articulate and link the somatic, visceral, sensory, and motoric aspects of the patient's experience to figures from early childhood and the affects associated with them. The fragments of the patient's inner world became integrated. She began to experience her body and mind as two inextricable aspects of an indivisible whole.

These observations raised questions that pertain not only to somatization, but also to the broader subject of the connection between body and mind. The first questions, those concerning somatization, focus on a reexamination of what is encoded in somatic symptoms. Are symptoms or the emphasis on bodily experience an early form of affect? Do symptoms appear in the course of an analysis when an affect state is newly mobilized? Are somatic symptoms or emphasized bodily states concrete referants as well as concretized symbols of invalidated and dissociated subjective experience?

Intimacy, Boundaries, and Countertransference in the Analytic Relationship

Estelle Shane PHD and Morton Shane MD

Morton Shane

1800 Fairburn Ave.
Suite 203
Los Angeles, CA 90025

Morton Shane  

To our minds, Ted Jacobs's unique contribution to the theory of technique is twofold. First, he reminds us that countertransference is inevitable and ubiquitous, always defying our efforts to transcend with any permanence its constant impact on, and infusion into, the analytic relationship. Second, he shows us how the analyst's use of his or her self, that is, the attention to one's own subjective experience in genetic depth, aids this nonetheless endless endeavor.

The creative and fluctuating tension between intimacy and boundaries in the therapeutic relationship that has been present throughout the history of psychoanalysis owes much of its force to the analyst's countertransference participation.

Psychoanalysis in Hungary in the Era of Communism and Postcommunism

György Hidas MD

György Hidas

H 1121 Budapest
Zugligeti út 10-12
Hungary

György Hidas  

The history of Hungarian psychoanalysis is closely interlaced with the twentieth century vicissitudes of the country itself. The Hungarian Psychoanalytical Association was founded in Budapest very early, in 1913, in the vivid spiritual atmosphere of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy. The Association was headed by Freud's disciple and friend, Sándor Ferenczi (1873-1933), and existed until 1948, the year when the Communist regime came to full power. In the group forming around Ferenczi were such prominent analysts as Istvan Hollos, Lajos Levy, Sándor Rado, Geza Roheim, Michael and Alice Balint, Imre Hermann and also Melanie Klein, who trained with Ferenczi.

The Association was composed not only of medical members; for example, an active participant was Ignotus, editor-in-chief of the leading literature journal of the age, Nyugat (West). And a deep penetration by psychoanalytic ideas is evident in the contemporary literature and culture of the period as in the writings of many outstanding personalities (Frigyes Karinthy, Mihály Babits, Dezsô Kosztolányi, Milán Füst, Attila József, Gyula Krudy).

In the Spring of 1919, after Hungary's defeat in World War I, a communist government came to power for a short while, strongly supported by progressive, leftist, mostly Jewish intellectuals.

Dr. Hidas is Supervising and Training Analyst at the Hungarian Psychoanalytical Society and President of the Sándor Ferenczi Society, Budapest.

James Grotstein MD

James Grotstein

522 Dalehurst Avenue
Los Angeles, CA 90024-2516

James Grotstein  

Summary

It is the thesis of this contribution that the psychoanalytic approach to the understanding of “mind” “body” problems should begin first by undoing the concept of their separation and then realizing that “mind” and “body” are convenient Cartesian artifices that disguise a fundamental unity and cooperative (as well as noncooperative) functioning of the individual. I consequently recommend the usage of mindbody and bodymind in order to address this area of investigation. I also posit that, in their phantasied disconnection, there exists an object relationship.

Stimulus Entrapment: On a Common Basis of Somatization

Russell Meares MD

Russell Meares

Darcy Road
Westmead NSW 2145
Australia

Russell Meares  

Somatization is often conceived as if it were a form of language in which bodily symptoms are symbols, expressive of states that, for some reason, cannot be communicated directly. Can we be confident in this? Consider, for example, the following clinical presentation.

Session after session, the patient tells the therapist of a multitude of physical complaints. Pain is prominent. There is a preoccupation with sensation coming from viscera, joints, skin, and other parts of the body. The patient speaks in a monotonous way, as if the therapist were not in the room. Indeed, the patient barely looks towards the therapist and appears to expect no responses. The descriptions of symptoms are accompanied by a catalogue of events concerning such matters as problems with work and family. The patient seems unable to imagine. Rather, he or she appears to be inextricably caught up in the experience of sensation and immediate events. Is this presentation a form of symbolic communication or is it a literal representation of the patient's experience at the time? The main thesis of this paper develops the latter view. The individual is seen as enmeshed in a system of “stimulus entrapment” (Meares, 1993). This clinical phenomenon is perhaps the commonest form of somatization confronting a psychotherapist. It can be conceived as a manifestation of a disruption in the sense of going on being, or self.

Dr. Meares is Professor of Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, University of Sydney, Australia.

The Suppression and Censorship of Ferenczi's Confusion of Tongues Paper

Arnold Rachman PHD

Arnold Rachman

10 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10016

Arnold Rachman  

I. The Confusion of Tongues (COT) Drama

The Confusion of Tongues paper could have ushered in a new era in psychoanalysis when Ferenczi delivered it in 1932, but it caused such an enormous controversy that the message it conveyed was lost in the battle to deliver and publish it. In actuality, the controversy surrounding the Confusion of Tongues paper constitutes one of the darkest moments in the history of psychoanalysis. At the time Ferenczi presented these ideas, he wished to have them accepted by Freud and the analytic community and integrated into mainstream psychoanalysis. But he was always ambivalent about his deviations from Freud and never seemed to realize how far he had deviated and how much he represented the first dissident point of view in psychoanalysis (Gedo, 1987, personal communication; Rachman, 1989b, 1997; Thompson, 1944).

There are many reasons Ferenczi didn't realize how far he had departed from what had become, by 1932, traditional psychoanalysis. Ferenczi continued to experiment, expand his thinking, and develop ways to elasticize the psychoanalytic situation. But Freud and his conservative followers did not experiment. The inner circle, the Society of Rings, functioned to maintain the status quo.

Dr. Rachman is Clinical Professor of Psychology, Derner Institute, Adelphi University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis; Founder, Sándor Ferenczi Institute, NYC; author, Sándor Ferenczi: The Psychotherapist of Tenderness and Compassion.

I am grateful to Ernst Falzeder, Ph.D., editor of the Freud/Ferenczi Correspondence, for his critical review of this manuscript.

[[RunningHead]]

The Capacity for Countertransference

Howard Levine MD

Howard Levine

124 Dean Road
Brookline, MA 02146

Howard Levine  

I

Although the concept of countertransference is a cornerstone of clinical psychoanalysis, one that is fundamental to the theory of analytic technique, the boundaries of its definition have remained open to debate. The analytic literature contains numerous efforts by various authors to widen or narrow the scope of the meaning of countertransference or to promote or discourage its relevance for clinical technique. So many contrasting views have been voiced that the term countertransference has come to suffer from overexpansion, attempts at overt and covert redefinition, a lack of precision, and an inconstancy of usage.

In considering the literature on countertransference, which is too extensive to summarize here (see, for example, Tyson, 1986, and Slakter, 1987), it becomes apparent that the use of the term by any given author will be determined by his/her stance in regard to four fundamental questions:

To what extent are the feelings, fantasies, and responses of the analyst in the analytic situation a function of the psychology of the analyst (e.g., Freud, 1910; Reich, 1951) or the patient (Heimann (1950)?

Should the term countertransference refer to a broad or narrow range of feelings and reactions in the analyst to the patient and the analytic situation?

Dr. Levine is Faculty, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute (BPSI); Faculty, Massachusetts Institute for Psychoanalysis (MIP).

The First Direct Analysis of Transference and Countertransference

Benjamin Wolstein PHD

Benjamin Wolstein

2 West 67th Street
New York, NY 10023

Benjamin Wolstein  

Psychoanalysis never takes place in the absence of interpretive beliefs and values. Based on this ineluctable fact, supremacy is often ascribed to the various perspectives on interpretive activity. Yet a number of other things does not take place in the absence of interpretive perspectives either—such as teaching, farming, motorcycle maintenance, not to mention all the other forms of psychotherapy in addition to psychoanalysis that take shape in an interpretive and speculative context. This holds, in my view, so long as the context of interpretation is not confused with the dynamics of experience being lived and worked through within that context. The existence of psychodynamics is not, itself, a product of interpretation. It arises in the direct experience of striving and feeling, thinking and imagining, saying and doing, that may or may may not be interpreted later. The preference for interpretive matters always comes down, finally to questions of choice, not only about the line of interpretation taken, but about the time and attention and energy devoted to it. Going beyond the empiric of clinical psychoanalytic inquiry is not always necessary, however.

Dr. Wolstein is a member of the faculties of the William Alanson White Institute and New York University.

An earlier draft of this paper, entitled “From Ferenczi's Mutual Analysis with R.N. to Coparticipant Psychoanalytic Therapy,” was presented at the Interpersonal-Humanist Colloqium of the Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, New York University, December 1991. It was also taped for the Master Lecture Series II, sponsored by the Continuing Professional Education Division, William Alanson White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis, and Psychology, July 1992.

The Primitive Psyche, Communication, and the Language of the Body

John Gedo MD

John Gedo

680 North Lake Shore Drive
Chicago, IL 60611

John Gedo  

Toward the end of the 19th century, students of human behavior, led by French psychiatrists such as Charcot and Bernheim, rediscovered that the Cartesian boundary between body and mind is far from being impermeable. As their disciple, Sigmund Freud, was later to put the matter, certain ideas tend, in specific contexts, to make a “mysterious leap” from mind to body. It is widely understood that psychoanalysis developed in a medical (and in particular a neurological) setting because the initial target of Freud's investigations (see Breuer and Freud, 1895) was hysteria, which was then viewed as a somatic syndrome. In Studies on Hysteria, Breuer reported his great discovery of 1881 that hysterical symptoms could be influenced through a “talking cure,” a finding that compelled the logical conclusion that such somatic symptoms represent a “conversion” of mental processes to the bodily realm.

As Freud's clinical procedures gradually evolved into the psychoanalytic method, it soon became evident that somatization can be observed in statu nascendi in the psychoanalytic setting itself. Ferenczi (1912) was the first to enunciate the concept that such temporary symptoms in the course of analysis amount to communications from patient to analyst; as he put this, the symptoms may “join in the conversation.

Dr. Gedo has contributed 15 books and over 125 articles to the psychoanalytic literature. He has been retired since 1994.

Susan Coates PHD and Mary Moore PHD

Mary Moore  

In this paper we will describe the case of Colin, a 312-year old boy who suffered significant trauma of a nonsexual nature, which occurred in the context of his primary attachment relationship. The case was the subject of an extended previous communication devoted to a psychodynamic understanding of gender identity disorder of childhood (Coates, Friedman, and Wolfe, 1991). Here we present the case, not with special reference to issues of gender, but as seen through the particular lens of trauma. Colin's traumatization can be conceptualized as having two different components, one entailing the precipitous loss of the emotional availability of his primary caretaker and the other entailing physical confrontations, experienced as potentially life-threatening, when he tried to reestablish contact with her. Beyond this, the case also touches on the issue of the cross-generational transfer of trauma.

To be noted at the outset is that neither what has been documented of Colin's traumatization nor the cross-generational issues involved in it were sexual in nature. Why present such a case in a special issue devoted to the topic of sexual abuse?

Susan Coates, Ph.D. is on the Faculty of the Columbia Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research and is an Associate Clinical Professor of Medical Psychology, in the Department of Psychiatry, College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia University.

Dr. Moore is Clinical Lecturer, Psychology Department, University of Colorado, Boulder, and Honorary Senior Psychotherapist, Child and Family Department, Tavistock Clinic, London.

21, Maresfield Gardens

Mary Target  

Recent years have seen increasingly informed media presentations of psychological principles and psychological treatments. Alternative therapeutic models (pharmacotherapy, behavioral, and cognitive behavioral treatments) have received considerable exposure as have critiques of psychoanalysis and the work of Freud. Perhaps as a consequence, there is increasing unease about the time and expense involved in psychoanalytic treatment, particularly for children, who do not generally choose to come for analysis. The common-sense view outside psychoanalytic circles is, increasingly, that psychoanalysis is no more effective than other forms of treatment, some would say less, yet it takes far longer and is substantially more expensive than, for instance, medication or cognitive-behavior therapy. The traditional view on this within psychoanalysis is that analysts know their form of treatment is effective and, in fact, unique in its effects and that there is no need to prove this. For those who think beyond this, there is often a further statement that it would, in any case, be impossible to prove the value of psychoanalysis, because the important aspects of both process and outcome are (while clear to analyst and patient) unmeasurable.

Symptoms and Symbols: A Multiple Code Theory of Somatization

Wilma Bucci PHD

Wilma Bucci

Garden City, NY 11530

Wilma Bucci  

The interaction of psychic and somatic processes has been a central concern of psychoanalysis from its initial formulations (Freud, 1895, 1900) to the present day. In contrast to Freud's time, the interaction of emotion and somatic illness is now also recognized in the medical field. It is not only the special disorders identified as hysterias, nor even the medical entities traditionally classified as psychosomatic that are affected by such interaction; the field of psychoneuroimmunology supports the view that

All disease is multifactoral and biopsychosocial in onset and course—the result of interrelationships among specific etiologic (e.g., bacteria, viruses, carcinogens), genetic, endocrine, nervous, immune, emotional, and behavioral factors [Solomon, 1987, p. 1].

The potential scope of psychoanalytic treatment is enormously expanded by these developments; the need for a coherent psychoanalytic theory is intensified as well, to bring psychological understanding of the interactions among cognition, emotion, and somatic functions in line with advances in the medical field.

Freud's metapsychology has failed as a basis for a modern scientific theory.

Difficulties in Maintaining an Analytic Stance in the Treatment of Adults Who Were Sexually Abused as Children

Howard Levine MD

Howard Levine

124 Dean Road
Brookline, MA 02146

Howard Levine  

Summary

In the course of this presentation, I have attempted to convey something of a stance and conceptual framework for the treatment of adults who were sexually abused in childhood, which I believe are consistently, some of my patients might say “determinedly,” analytic. While the exact definition of all that this stance entails is subject to debate, at its core is an inexorable commitment to thoughtful and respectful inquiry into the experience of both participants in the therapeutic setting. Above all, I believe that the analytic stance is a way of looking at, exploring and trying to make sense of internal experience. It is an inherent component of how we, as analytic therapists, try to think and behave in the clinical situation. It encompasses an attempt at thinking, rather than acting, and is more closely allied to the realm of the symbolic, psychic reality, delay of gratification, and renunciation of and mourning for what was lost or what cannot be than to the realm of the concrete, material reality; immediate gratification; and the refusal and/or denial of the inevitability and necessity of renunciation and mourning.

In discussing the treatment situation, I have tried to show how all therapy mobilizes and even relies upon powerful forces that tend to move both patient and analyst away from an analytic stance. Adults who were sexually abused in childhood are no exception. Instead, the various forms of ego disturbance, to which their traumatic past may contribute, only make them more likely to relate via enactment and projective identification. This presents important implications, many of which I have attempted to discuss, for the treatment relationship—transference and countertransference—and for technique.

Dispensing with archaic views of affects and looking at emotions from the point of view of information processing and incorporating up-to-date understanding of the interaction of the various components of adult-type emotions, we need to keep in mind the several aspects of affect that play a role in the genesis and maintenance of psychosomatic diseases. First is the cognitive element of emotion, every emotion having its own meaning. Both fear and anxiety signal that something bad is about to happen. Fear alerts us to external, veridical, and avoidable danger, whereas anxiety relates to danger that is usually unconscious, and as analytic therapists we search for its meaning by investigating associations and transferences. Depression signals that something bad has happened and we are inclined to attribute the cause to ourselves and/or condemn ourselves for helplessness to prevent it. In anger/rage we feel that a bad thing has been done by a bad object whom we are entitled to hate and punish.

Secondly, the psychological aspects of emotions are not “expressive” as previously thought in reference to the economic view of psychoanalysis, nor are they connected on a one-to-one basis, anxiety with the sympathetic nervous system and depression with parasympathetic (and allegedly conservatory) system. A trace of this kind of thinking can be found in Engel's (1962) term “depression-withdrawal.

On Progenitors and Why We Choose Them

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 18th Street, NW
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

My mentor in psychiatry and psychoanalysis was Dr. Lewis Hill. I call him my mentor because, while I had many teachers, Lewis was more than a conduit to learning; he was a facilitator to growth. Lewis combined in one person contradictory traits that I was familiar with since childhood and had spent years struggling to reconcile satisfactorily. With his shortcropped brown hair and somewhat stiff posture, Lewis could give an impression of a transplanted Prussian general. This side of him translated into a no-nonsense, uncompromising stance on the side of doing what was necessary for the safety, welfare, and recovery of our patients at Sheppard Pratt Hospital.

His other trait was his exquisite sensitivity to the patient's inner world as the patient perceived it, especially the patient's vulnerability to painful affect. At a time when psychotic patients were universally regarded as defending against murderous discharges of aggressive drive, Lewis emphasized that careful observation might reveal the patient's significant problem to be chronic shyness or repeated experiences of humiliation or a persistent failure to fulfill a desire to find a way to be close to someone. At a time when abstinence and neutrality were extolled as central to the pursuit of insight (Stone, 1961), Lewis believed that what an analyst communicated about his inner self and his therapeutic intent transcended technique as a factor in recovery (Hill, 1955).

Dr. Lichtenberg is Editor-in-Chief, Psychoanalytic Inquiry; Faculty member, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, and Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Georgetown University.

The study of childhood trauma and the field of psychoanalysis can be compared to a little boy and little girl who grew up next door to each other. Judith Vida MD

Judith Vida

301 S. Fair Oaks Avenue
Suite 406A
Pasadena, CA 91105

Judith Vida  

The impetus for this article came from an invitation to join a panel that had as its subject the use of the voice in the psychoanalytic process. In approaching this subject from the perspective of the life and work of Sándor Ferenczi (1873-1933), which has been my principal research interest, I began to think about “the Voice.” Because Ferenczi had been passionately attentive to the metacommunications of the analytic situation, I thought it was likely that a longitudinal examination of his work would yield something worthwhile related to the topic, and this quickly proved to be true. Summary

In Germany, it has been demonstrated that psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapeutic/psychosomatic inpatient treatment of an average of 7 to 8 weeks' duration is not only effective but also contributes to considerable cost savings both within the health system and the pension system.

It might be surprising, therefore, that the future existence of this system in Germany is threatened. In the last few years, the overall national economic situation has deteriorated, along with an enormous rise in social welfare costs. Measures that are being uncritically used to cut down on public expenditures for inpatient treatment in general may well lead to restrictions for inpatient psychotherapeutic treatment as well. In addition, a marked shift away from psychoanalytic methods

Only the future will show if psychoanalytic psychotherapy, claiming the successes of the past, will manage to overcome the challenges of time and of the Zeitgeist.

Summary

Somatic memories were defined as virtual mental states unarticulated and unintegrated with the cognitive and affective components of the traumatic experiences. The preponderance of somatic manifestations in the early emergence of memories of childhood sexual abuse was accounted for as follows: 1) the trauma was somatic in nature to begin with and was encoded, stored, and retrieved in memory along somaticsensory channels; 2) the physical dimension of the trauma was an intensive foreground experience; 3) the original experience was never articulated beyond the level of the physical aspect; and 4) the somatic nature of the memories concretized and validated the reality of the traumatic experience.

A case was presented of a woman who recovered memories of early, severe, and chronic childhood sexual abuse during the course of analysis. This clinical material illustrated the prevalence of somatic manifestations in the early stages of memory retrieval. The material also demonstrated the establishment and evolution of a deepening validating intersubjective tie with the analyst that was crucial to the emergence of the traumatic recollections. The case material traced the diminution of the dissociative process and the growing cognitive and affective awareness achieved by the patient as she integrated her newly discovered reality into her ongoing self-organization.

Sharon Kahn  

Freud May have been one of those who “disturbed the sleep of the world” (Freud, 1914), but it was Ferenczi who disturbed the sleep of the analytic community. While Freud originated the Oedipal theory as a psychoanalytic developmental drama, Ferenczi rendered conscious the oedipal drama within the analytic community by posing a cardinal question: With whom would they align—the captives or the kings? Would they intrepidly investigate and empathically identify with their patients' vulnerabilities, or would they impassively identify with the aggressors and refer to their patients' traumas as childhood fantasies?

Ferenczi unambiguously cast himself on the side of the patient, referring to the therapeutic process as one where both sides abdicate “authority … they give the impression of two equally terrified children who compare their experiences, and because of their common fate understand each other completely and instinctively try to comfort each other” (Ferenczi, 1988, p. 56). Ferenczi, out of this alignment with his patients, went further than merely appreciating and validating their unique trauma-begotten insights into the real person of their analyst, who is a flawed person (Ferenczi, 1932, 1988). He experimented with the parameters of the psychoanalytic setting to forge mutual analyses with his patients.

Ferenczi's experiments with mutual analysis may have been influenced in part out of his personal difficulties with Freud.

Current research and reflection are bringing new understanding of the meaning and impact of patient-therapist sexual relations. To some degree, this comes from recognizing the similarities this phenomenon bears to childhood sexual abuse and rape. All are life-changing, traumatic, and damaging events that occur in significantly power-imbalanced relationships. While there is finally recognition that it is neither productive nor appropriate to blame the victim, we have not yet established a culture in which victims are freed from self-blame and allowed to believe that patient-therapist sex is always the responsibility of the therapist.

As a victim of sexual abuse by a psychotherapist and as one who has, over the past 8 years, come into contact with several hundred other victims, I present a victim's perspective of what happens, why it happens, and what we in the victim community believe the professional and lay communities can do, on both the micro and macro levels, to continue to change the existing culture. Because I am not a therapist, this article is descriptive rather than interpretive.

An analysis of the phenomenon of patient-therapist sex must ultimately focus on process, impact, and healing, rather than on patient pathology or behavior.

For a Metapsychology of the Psychoanalyst: Sándor Ferenczi's Quest

André Haynal MD

André Haynal

20 B, Gradelle
CH-1224 Geneva
Switzerland

André Haynal  

I

“The young child is familiar with much knowledge … that later becomes buried by the forces of repression” (Ferenczi, 1923 [257], p. 350).1 Small children are often amusing because they put into words—sometimes a bit awkwardly—what they (still) perceive without repressing; adults for whom the same material has already been repressed then receive their words as a kind of revelation. The effect can either be the amusement of liberation—a sort of “aha!” experience—or, because of their own repression, one that creates tension and even hostility: “How stupid!” or “One doesn't say things like that!” which corresponds to an intention to reinforce the adult's repression and at the same time to inculcate in the child the “do-not-say,” indeed the “do-not-think.”

“Wise baby”—he himself used the English term in the German text (Ferenczi, 1923 [257] and Ferenczi, 1932 [308], p. 274)—is what Ferenczi was to remain all his life. In that, he differed from his fellow pioneers and even from his master, Freud.

Dr. Haynal is Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Geneva; Training and Supervising Analyst and Former President of the Swiss Psychoanalytical Society.

Translated from the French by Linda Butler, Washington, DC.

Response to the Contributors to “Essays Inspired by Theodore Jacobs's The Use of the Self”

Theodore Jacobs MD

Theodore Jacobs

170 East 77th St.
Apt. 1G
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Jacobs  

I am honored to have had The Use of the Self chosen as the subject of this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and grateful to the contributors who so generously took time from their busy schedules to write essays for this volume. I owe a debt of thanks, too, to Dr. Melvin Bornstein, who organized the issue and did so splendid a job editing it.

It is a rare privilege for an author to be able to review a collection of articles by distinguished colleagues that have been written in response to his work. One feels especially privileged when, as is true of the articles in this issue, each of them makes a significant contribution in its own right. Having had the opportunity to view my book through the lenses provided by my colleagues has been an invaluable experience for me. Not only have I gained a fresh perspective on my work and been stimulated to review my thinking in a number of areas, I have also learned a great deal from my colleagues. Utilizing some of the ideas concerning countertransference, the analyst's subjectivity, and the interactive aspect of the analytic process that I and others have written about, several of these colleagues have extended these ideas, pursued their theoretical implications beyond the point that I had carried them, and broken new ground.

Dr. Jacobs is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine; Training and Supervising Analyst, New York Psychoanalytic Institute and Psychoanalytic Institute at New York University; and a member of the editorial board, Psychoanalytic Quarterly.

The Supervisorial Situation: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Factors Influencing Transference and Countertransference Themes

Alan Skolnikoff MD

Alan Skolnikoff

205 Edgewood Avenue
San Francisco, CA 94117

Alan Skolnikoff  

Summary

In this paper, I have discussed various elements of the supervisorial situation, with a focus on the transference and countertransference reactions of the supervisor and supervisee. I have reviewed how an understanding of the supervisorial situation has evolved and how it is now useful to look at interactive factors between supervisor, supervisee, and patient. I have expanded on how many models of psychoanalytic process have their counterparts in the supervisorial process. In addition, I have outlined extrinsic factors in diagrammatic form to show how the supervisorial process is influenced by the training analyst and the Institute. In the spirit of Ted Jacobs's expanding our thinking about the analyst's use of his emotional reactions to understand his patient, I have applied analogous thoughts about how the supervisor, through self-inquiry, can expand his thinking about the supervisorial process.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Perhaps the last two decades will be seen as a period in the history of psychoanalysis when attention was finally directed to the analyst in the analytic situation. Because of a relativistic view of reality, the development of conceptual tools that account for narcissism, object relations, development, and almost a century of clinical experience have resulted in a modification of the analyst's role in the treatment situation. The consequence has been for analysts to scrutinize themselves more carefully than they had previously.

An outstanding exemplar of this trend is Theodore J. Jacobs's book The Use of the Self (the “self” in the title refers to the analyst), a series of essays based on papers Jacobs has written over the last decade.

Historically, the criteria used by the American Psychoanalytic Association for granting certification focused on the applicant's ability to convey an understanding of the patient's mental state in the analytic process. During the last 8 years these criteria were expanded to include the applicant's understanding of the analyst's contribution to the analytic process.

Accordingly, we thought it would be useful to devote an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry to the exploration of how Jacobs's ideas regarding the experience of the analyst have been elaborated during the last decade.

In the introduction to The Use of the Self, Jacobs outlines the origin of his interests as a reaction to a prevailing opinion that countertransference represented a problem of the analyst that required repair. This view made it impossible to confront and discuss the analyst's experience as modes of communication that could promote the analytic process.

Jacobs states that central to his views of the analyst's role is the concept of the analyzing instrument. The concept is associated with Isakower, who based his thinking on Freud's metaphor of the analyst who must turn his unconscious like a receiver to the transmitter of the patient's unconscious.

The Discovery of the Budapest Writings

Claude Lorin PHD

Claude Lorin

Claude Lorin  

“It's pure gold” said Freud about Sándor Ferenczi's articles (Freud, 1933). He was referring most certainly to the dense, original writings that the Hungarian psychoanalyst had been lovingly preparing for discovery since their first meeting in 1908. I had read Ferenczi's psychoanalytic works and felt that he had a different concept—one that came from a forgotten lineage that needed to be restored to history. Thus, with this great dream overshadowing my small passion, I decided to leave for Hungary in August 1976. I was encouraged by my own analyst in this spiritual migration to discover the unpublished writings. In Paris, rumor had it that they had been broken up and might no longer exist. Therefore, with neither a specific assignment nor any other great illusion, I left to explore the Budapest writings. What irritated me profoundly was that the destiny of these writings, about which we knew so little, could be of so little interest to some.

So, first to Budapest via Vienna (where Sándor had practiced medicine) and then Vác and Esztergom, where I met Györgyi Kurcz. She was delighted to hear a little “talk about France.” On to Bakony with its wild forest in which I lost my way, left me with rough memories of roving shadows that leaned toward me and make strange noises in the clear blue evening. Permeated with my studies of Novalis, Shelling, and Goethe at Nanterre, I imagined the King of the Aulnis. In the region of the Balaton Lake, I could feel the presence of spirits which increased my understanding of Ferenczi's interest in “spiritism.

Dr. Lorin is Professor of Psychology, University of Reims; in private practice, Paris.
